parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 8. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a supervisor at a cinema talking to a new member of staff on her first day at work. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 6. Rhys: Hello, you must be Lucy. I'm Rhys, one of the duty supervisors. Welcome to the Regal Cinema. Lucy: Hi. Nice to meet you. Sorry, is that Reece, R, E, E, C, E? Rhys: No, it's spelled R, H, Y, S. It's a Welsh name. People often spell it wrong on the staff rota, so don't worry if you see it written differently. Lucy: R, H, Y, S. I'll remember that. Rhys: Thanks. So, have you worked in a cinema before? Lucy: No, but I worked in a cafe for two summers, so I'm used to dealing with customers. And I love films, so this seemed like the perfect job. Rhys: Well, you'll certainly see plenty of them here. We've got six screens, and on a busy Saturday we can have over two thousand customers. Rhys: So, there are a few practical things to sort out first, and then I'll show you around and explain what you'll be doing today. Lucy: Great. The email said I should arrive half an hour before my shift starts. Rhys: That's right. You'll always need a bit of time to get ready. First of all, the staff room. It's through that door behind the ticket desk. There's a big cupboard in there where you can put your coat and bag. It isn't locked, though, so don't leave anything valuable in your pockets. Lucy: OK. Can I keep my phone with me? Rhys: Yes, as long as it's switched off while you're working. Lucy: Fine. Rhys: Next, you need to see Nina in the office. She's the manager. She'll need two passport photos from you. They're for your staff ID card, which you'll need to get into the building each day. Lucy: I've got them here in my bag. Rhys: Perfect. She'll also give you a name badge. We don't have a uniform here. Everyone just wears their own black clothes, but you must wear your badge at all times, so that customers know who to ask for help. Lucy: Right. And where's the office? Rhys: It's upstairs. The first floor is where the cafe is, and the office is above that, on the second floor. There's a lift, but staff are supposed to use the stairs. Lucy: The second floor. Got it. Rhys: Oh, and one more thing. All staff get a discount on food and drinks in the cafe. It used to be ten per cent, but it's just gone up to twenty. Lucy: Oh, that's nice. Rhys: And you can watch films for free on your days off, as long as there are seats available. Lucy: That's a great perk. Do I need to book a seat in advance? Rhys: Just ask at the ticket desk on the day. They'll give you a staff ticket if there's space. New releases are often full at the weekend, though, so it's best to go on a weekday. Lucy: OK, I'll remember that. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 7 to 10. Rhys: Now, let me explain your jobs for today. You'll be working in three areas. First, the screens. After each film finishes, you'll need to go in and check the rows for litter and anything people have left behind. The lights aren't very bright, so you'll need to use a torch to look under the seats. Lucy: Do people leave much behind? Rhys: You'd be surprised. Umbrellas, scarves, phones. Anything valuable goes straight to the ticket desk, and we write it down in the lost property book. Lucy: OK. Rhys: Then, between films, you'll help on the snack counter. The staff there serve the customers, but your job will be to keep the popcorn machine full. It runs out very quickly, especially on Saturdays. You don't need to worry about the drinks machine. The counter staff look after that themselves. Lucy: Right. Rhys: The third area is the ticket barrier, at the entrance to the screens. You'll check people's tickets and show them which screen to go to. Please also remind every customer that their phone must be switched to silent before the film starts. We get a lot of complaints about phones ringing in the middle of films. Lucy: I can imagine. Rhys: Finally, safety. Before your shift ends today, I'd like you to walk round the building with me and learn where all the fire exits are. If there's ever an emergency, staff have to guide customers out quickly. Lucy: That makes sense. Is there anything else I should be careful about? Rhys: Just stay polite, even if customers are rude. And ask me if you're not sure about anything. Most people are lovely, but occasionally someone gets upset if a film is sold out or starts late. If that happens, just call me on the radio and I'll come and sort it out. You'll get your radio from the ticket desk at the start of each shift. Lucy: Thanks, Rhys. I'm really looking forward to it. That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a swimming coach giving advice about open water swimming in a podcast, and talking about her club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Megan: Hello, and welcome to my podcast. I'm Megan Hale, and I'm a coach with Lakeside Open Water Swimmers. Over the last few years, swimming outdoors in lakes, rivers and the sea has become hugely popular, and every week I hear from people who'd love to give it a try but aren't sure where to start. Our club meets at a reservoir just outside the town, where there are lifeguards on duty every weekend from April to October. Megan: There are lots of free training plans online which promise to take you from swimming a few lengths of a pool to swimming a mile outdoors. Some of them are very good, and they're easy to follow. The trouble is that most of them were written for pool swimmers, and they say very little about the ways in which open water is different. They don't warn you about things like cold water shock, the gasping reaction that happens when you first get into cold water, which can be really dangerous if you're not prepared for it. Megan: And if you have a heart condition or high blood pressure, those plans aren't suitable at all, because cold water puts extra strain on the heart. Anyone with a medical condition like that should always talk to their doctor before they start. It's also worth remembering that the plans usually assume you'll be swimming in calm, clear water, and that's rarely the case outdoors, where there may be waves, currents and weeds. Megan: Now, a few tips. People often assume they need to buy an expensive wetsuit straight away. Actually, many of our members swim without one, and I'd suggest you wait until you know you're going to stick with it. What's really important is to get used to the cold gradually. Start in late spring or summer, when the water's warmer, and keep swimming as it gets colder, so that your body has time to adapt. And always wear a brightly coloured swimming hat, so that boats and other people can see you easily. Please never swim alone, even if you're experienced, and don't eat a large meal just before you go in. Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Megan: People give all sorts of reasons for not joining us sooner. Owen joined last year, although he'd been thinking about it for ages. He's a good swimmer, and he's had plenty of free time since he retired, but he simply couldn't bear the idea of being cold. Now he swims all through the winter, and he says it's the best part of his week. Megan: Priya, on the other hand, loved the idea of swimming outdoors, and the cold didn't bother her at all. But she'd only ever swum a few lengths in a pool, and she was convinced she wasn't a strong enough swimmer to keep up with everyone else. She was amazed to find that we have groups for every level. Megan: Dan had wanted to join for years, but he works shifts at the hospital, and our sessions always seemed to clash with his work. Now that we've added early morning swims, he comes whenever his rota allows. Megan: Rosa grew up by the sea and has always been a confident swimmer. But when she was a teenager, she had a frightening experience in very cold water, when she couldn't catch her breath, and after that she avoided cold water completely. With our help, she's gradually built up her tolerance, and she now swims all year round. Megan: As for me, I only started open water swimming ten years ago. My first long swim was across a five kilometre lake. My sister had done it the year before, and I wanted to prove that I could do it too. I'd trained for months, but after about two kilometres I was exhausted, and I seriously thought about stopping. It was a volunteer in a kayak beside me who kept encouraging me, and eventually I made it to the other side. Megan: Signing up for an organised swim is a great way to stay motivated. Some people enter one as soon as they join the club, but I think that's too soon. On the other hand, you don't need to wait a whole year. After a couple of months of regular swimming, most people are ready for a short event of about one kilometre, and it gives you something to aim for. Well, I hope that's given you some ideas. See you in the water! That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two students, Amelia and Ryan, talking about houseplants. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Ryan: So, Amelia, you're off to Spain next month for your work placement? Amelia: Yes, I can't wait. But I've got a problem. I've got about fifteen plants in my room, and I can't take them with me. I was wondering if you'd look after some of them while I'm away. Ryan: Sure, I'd be happy to. But I'm warning you, I'm not very good with plants. The last one I had died in about a month. Amelia: Don't worry. My grandmother runs a plant nursery, and she's given me loads of advice. The most important thing, she says, is not to overwater them. Most people kill their plants by giving them too much water, not too little. You should wait until the top of the soil feels dry before you water them again. Ryan: Well, that seems obvious when you think about it. Plants in the wild don't get watered every day. Amelia: And she says to water them much less in winter, because they're hardly growing then. Ryan: That makes sense too. I'll try to remember that. Amelia: The one I'm most worried about is the big cactus on my desk. It's really old. My grandmother gave it to me when I left home to come to university, and it had been on her kitchen windowsill for about thirty years before that. Ryan: Wow. So is it quite valuable? Amelia: Not in terms of money. You could buy one like it for a few pounds. But every time I look at it, I think of her kitchen and all the time I spent there as a child. I couldn't bear it if anything happened to it. Ryan: I'll take special care of it, then. Where should I put the plants, though? My room doesn't get much sun. Amelia: That depends on the plant. Grandma says the biggest mistake people make is putting plants wherever they look nice, instead of thinking about how much light each one needs. The cactus needs as much sun as possible, so it should go in the kitchen, but the ferns would be fine in your room. Ryan: So it's about choosing the right place for each plant, rather than just using them as decoration. Amelia: Exactly. Some of them will also need bigger pots in the spring. You have to be really careful when you repot them. When I was about seven, I tried to repot one of Grandma's plants on my own, and I pulled it out by the stem and snapped it in half. I was so upset. She wasn't angry at all, but she showed me how to do it properly, holding the base of the plant and turning the pot upside down. I've never forgotten it. Ryan: I'll bear that in mind. You know, I might buy a few plants myself while you're away. Those really big ones look amazing, but they're so expensive. Amelia: I know. A large fig tree can cost over a hundred pounds. Most students just can't afford that. That's why Grandma always says to start with small plants. They grow surprisingly quickly anyway. Ryan: Good point. Ryan: Is there anything else I need to know before you go? Amelia: Just talk to them now and then. Grandma swears it helps, although I'm not sure there's any scientific evidence for that! Ryan: I'll give it a try. It can't do any harm. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Ryan: I'd love to visit your grandmother's nursery. What's it like? Amelia: It's quite big. There's a main building with a cafe, a huge greenhouse, a polytunnel and an outdoor area with trees and shrubs. The heavy things, like bags of compost, are sold from a shed next to the car park, so people don't have to carry them far. Ryan: I suppose she has some rare plants? Amelia: Yes, some very unusual ones. You'd think she'd hide them away in the greenhouse, but she likes customers to see them. So she puts them on the very top shelves in the main building, where you have to ask a member of staff to reach them for you. Ryan: Clever. That way nobody can just walk off with them. Amelia: Exactly. Ryan: Does she do anything for children? Amelia: Oh, yes. She runs a gardening club for local kids, and she's built a special area just for them, with low tables and small tools, where they grow their own seedlings and look after them every week. Ryan: That's lovely. Amelia: And people are always giving her cuttings from their own plants, far more than she could ever sell. So she puts them in a box by the entrance gate, and customers can take them for free. Ryan: What about people who order plants in advance? Amelia: Those are kept right at the back of the site, so they don't get mixed up with the plants that are for sale. Customers just collect them from there when they're ready. Ryan: And houseplants? That's what I'd be looking for. Amelia: She used to keep those in the greenhouse, but it got far too hot in summer. So now they're all in the cafe, on shelves around the walls, and people can choose them while they have a coffee. Ryan: What a great idea. You'll have to take me there when you get back from Spain. Amelia: Definitely. She'd love to meet the person who's been looking after her cactus! That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental studies lecture about the reintroduction of beavers to Britain. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about the reintroduction of beavers to Britain, which has become one of the most widely discussed conservation projects of recent years. The Eurasian beaver was once common across the country, but it was hunted for its fur, for its meat, and for a substance produced by its scent glands, which was used in medicine and perfume. By the sixteenth century, beavers had disappeared from Britain altogether, and for more than four hundred years there were none living in the wild. Lecturer: Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers, because they change their environment more dramatically than almost any other animal apart from humans. By building dams across streams, they create ponds and wetlands. These slow down the flow of water after heavy rain, which can reduce the risk of flooding in towns and villages further downstream. The ponds also trap soil that has been washed off farmland, along with the chemicals it contains, so the water that flows out of beaver wetlands is often much cleaner than the water that flows in. A single family of beavers can build several dams along a short stretch of stream, and over time these can turn a narrow, fast-flowing channel into a complex network of pools and channels. Lecturer: The wetlands themselves support a huge variety of wildlife. Numbers of amphibians such as frogs increase, as do insects, and the insects in turn attract bats, which can often be seen hunting over beaver ponds at dusk. Some studies have found many more species living along streams with beavers than along similar streams without them. Dead trees standing in the water also provide nesting sites for birds such as woodpeckers. Lecturer: However, releasing beavers needs careful planning. The first requirement is a site with a good supply of food. Contrary to popular belief, beavers don't eat fish. They're vegetarian, and in winter they depend largely on the bark of trees, especially willow, which grows quickly and regrows after it has been cut. Secondly, it's essential to talk to farmers before any release takes place. Beaver dams can flood fields, and beavers sometimes feed on crops, so farmers need to know what to expect and how any problems will be dealt with. It's also important to check that the river system is large enough to support several families, because young beavers leave home at around two years old and need to find territories of their own. Lecturer: Beavers can also cause trouble by blocking drains under roads, which can lead to flooding in the wrong places. Fortunately, there are solutions. One of the most effective is to install pipes through the dam, which control the level of water in the pond without the dam having to be removed altogether. Lecturer: Now let's look at two examples. In 2013, a family of wild beavers was discovered living on the River Otter in Devon, in south-west England. Nobody knows exactly where they came from, but they're thought to have escaped from a private collection. The government agreed to a five-year trial, and the results were so positive that in 2020 the beavers were given permission to stay permanently, making them the first legally recognised wild population in England. Researchers found that the dams had reduced peak water flows during storms, helping to protect a village downstream. They also found that the beavers had brought new income to the area, thanks to an increase in tourism, as people came from all over the country hoping to catch a glimpse of them. Lecturer: In Scotland, beavers were officially reintroduced in Argyll in 2009, and in 2019 they became a legally protected species there. One of the most successful aspects of the Scottish projects has been the involvement of local communities. Volunteers help to monitor the beavers using cameras hidden near their lodges and dams, which record their activity at night, and local schools use the footage in their lessons. This kind of involvement helps people to feel that the beavers belong to them, and that makes a real difference when conflicts arise. In the second half of the lecture, we'll look at some of those conflicts in more detail. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

We get a lot of complaints about phones ringing in the middle of films. Lucy: I can imagine. Rhys: Finally, safety. Before your shift ends today, I'd like you to walk round the building with me and learn where all the fire exits are. If there's ever an emergency, staff have to guide customers out quickly. Lucy: That makes sense. Is there anything else I should be careful about? Rhys: Just stay polite, even if customers are rude. And ask me if you're not sure about anything. Most people are lovely, but occasionally someone gets upset if a film is sold out or starts late. If that happens, just call me on the radio and I'll come and sort it out. You'll get your radio from the ticket desk at the start of each shift. Lucy: Thanks, Rhys. I'm really looking forward to it. That is the end of Part 1. parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a swimming coach giving advice about open water swimming in a podcast, and talking about her club. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Megan: Hello, and welcome to my podcast. I'm Megan Hale, and I'm a coach with Lakeside Open Water Swimmers. Over the last few years, swimming outdoors in lakes, rivers and the sea has become hugely popular, and every week I hear from people who'd love to give it a try but aren't sure where to start. Our club meets at a reservoir just outside the town, where there are lifeguards on duty every weekend from April to October. Megan: There are lots of free training plans online which promise to take you from swimming a few lengths of a pool to swimming a mile outdoors. Some of them are very good, and they're easy to follow. The trouble is that most of them were written for pool swimmers, and they say very little about the ways in which open water is different. They don't warn you about things like cold water shock, the gasping reaction that happens when you first get into cold water, which can be really dangerous if you're not prepared for it. Megan: And if you have a heart condition or high blood pressure, those plans aren't suitable at all, because cold water puts extra strain on the heart. Anyone with a medical condition like that should always talk to their doctor before they start. It's also worth remembering that the plans usually assume you'll be swimming in calm, clear water, and that's rarely the case outdoors, where there may be waves, currents and weeds. Megan: Now, a few tips. People often assume they need to buy an expensive wetsuit straight away. Actually, many of our members swim without one, and I'd suggest you wait until you know you're going to stick with it. What's really important is to get used to the cold gradually. Start in late spring or summer, when the water's warmer, and keep swimming as it gets colder, so that your body has time to adapt. And always wear a brightly coloured swimming hat, so that boats and other people can see you easily. Please never swim alone, even if you're experienced, and don't eat a large meal just before you go in. Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Megan: People give all sorts of reasons for not joining us sooner. Owen joined last year, although he'd been thinking about it for ages. He's a good swimmer, and he's had plenty of free time since he retired, but he simply couldn't bear the idea of being cold. Now he swims all through the winter, and he says it's the best part of his week. Megan: Priya, on the other hand, loved the idea of swimming outdoors, and the cold didn't bother her at all. But she'd only ever swum a few lengths in a pool, and she was convinced she wasn't a strong enough swimmer to keep up with everyone else. She was amazed to find that we have groups for every level. Megan: Dan had wanted to join for years, but he works shifts at the hospital, and our sessions always seemed to clash with his work. Now that we've added early morning swims, he comes whenever his rota allows. Megan: Rosa grew up by the sea and has always been a confident swimmer. But when she was a teenager, she had a frightening experience in very cold water, when she couldn't catch her breath, and after that she avoided cold water completely. With our help, she's gradually built up her tolerance, and she now swims all year round. Megan: As for me, I only started open water swimming ten years ago. My first long swim was across a five kilometre lake. My sister had done it the year before, and I wanted to prove that I could do it too. I'd trained for months, but after about two kilometres I was exhausted, and I seriously thought about stopping. It was a volunteer in a kayak beside me who kept encouraging me, and eventually I made it to the other side. Megan: Signing up for an organised swim is a great way to stay motivated. Some people enter one as soon as they join the club, but I think that's too soon. On the other hand, you don't need to wait a whole year. After a couple of months of regular swimming, most people are ready for a short event of about one kilometre, and it gives you something to aim for. Well, I hope that's given you some ideas. See you in the water! That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two students, Amelia and Ryan, talking about houseplants. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25. Ryan: So, Amelia, you're off to Spain next month for your work placement? Amelia: Yes, I can't wait. But I've got a problem. I've got about fifteen plants in my room, and I can't take them with me. I was wondering if you'd look after some of them while I'm away. Ryan: Sure, I'd be happy to. But I'm warning you, I'm not very good with plants. The last one I had died in about a month. Amelia: Don't worry. My grandmother runs a plant nursery, and she's given me loads of advice. The most important thing, she says, is not to overwater them. Most people kill their plants by giving them too much water, not too little. You should wait until the top of the soil feels dry before you water them again. Ryan: Well, that seems obvious when you think about it. Plants in the wild don't get watered every day. Amelia: And she says to water them much less in winter, because they're hardly growing then. Ryan: That makes sense too. I'll try to remember that. Amelia: The one I'm most worried about is the big cactus on my desk. It's really old. My grandmother gave it to me when I left home to come to university, and it had been on her kitchen windowsill for about thirty years before that. Ryan: Wow. So is it quite valuable? Amelia: Not in terms of money. You could buy one like it for a few pounds. But every time I look at it, I think of her kitchen and all the time I spent there as a child. I couldn't bear it if anything happened to it. Ryan: I'll take special care of it, then. Where should I put the plants, though? My room doesn't get much sun. Amelia: That depends on the plant. Grandma says the biggest mistake people make is putting plants wherever they look nice, instead of thinking about how much light each one needs. The cactus needs as much sun as possible, so it should go in the kitchen, but the ferns would be fine in your room. Ryan: So it's about choosing the right place for each plant, rather than just using them as decoration. Amelia: Exactly. Some of them will also need bigger pots in the spring. You have to be really careful when you repot them. When I was about seven, I tried to repot one of Grandma's plants on my own, and I pulled it out by the stem and snapped it in half. I was so upset. She wasn't angry at all, but she showed me how to do it properly, holding the base of the plant and turning the pot upside down. I've never forgotten it. Ryan: I'll bear that in mind. You know, I might buy a few plants myself while you're away. Those really big ones look amazing, but they're so expensive. Amelia: I know. A large fig tree can cost over a hundred pounds. Most students just can't afford that. That's why Grandma always says to start with small plants. They grow surprisingly quickly anyway. Ryan: Good point. Ryan: Is there anything else I need to know before you go? Amelia: Just talk to them now and then. Grandma swears it helps, although I'm not sure there's any scientific evidence for that! Ryan: I'll give it a try. It can't do any harm. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30. Ryan: I'd love to visit your grandmother's nursery. What's it like? Amelia: It's quite big. There's a main building with a cafe, a huge greenhouse, a polytunnel and an outdoor area with trees and shrubs. The heavy things, like bags of compost, are sold from a shed next to the car park, so people don't have to carry them far. Ryan: I suppose she has some rare plants? Amelia: Yes, some very unusual ones. You'd think she'd hide them away in the greenhouse, but she likes customers to see them. So she puts them on the very top shelves in the main building, where you have to ask a member of staff to reach them for you. Ryan: Clever. That way nobody can just walk off with them. Amelia: Exactly. Ryan: Does she do anything for children? Amelia: Oh, yes. She runs a gardening club for local kids, and she's built a special area just for them, with low tables and small tools, where they grow their own seedlings and look after them every week. Ryan: That's lovely. Amelia: And people are always giving her cuttings from their own plants, far more than she could ever sell. So she puts them in a box by the entrance gate, and customers can take them for free. Ryan: What about people who order plants in advance? Amelia: Those are kept right at the back of the site, so they don't get mixed up with the plants that are for sale. Customers just collect them from there when they're ready. Ryan: And houseplants? That's what I'd be looking for. Amelia: She used to keep those in the greenhouse, but it got far too hot in summer. So now they're all in the cafe, on shelves around the walls, and people can choose them while they have a coffee. Ryan: What a great idea. You'll have to take me there when you get back from Spain. Amelia: Definitely. She'd love to meet the person who's been looking after her cactus! That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear part of an environmental studies lecture about the reintroduction of beavers to Britain. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Today I'm going to talk about the reintroduction of beavers to Britain, which has become one of the most widely discussed conservation projects of recent years. The Eurasian beaver was once common across the country, but it was hunted for its fur, for its meat, and for a substance produced by its scent glands, which was used in medicine and perfume. By the sixteenth century, beavers had disappeared from Britain altogether, and for more than four hundred years there were none living in the wild. Lecturer: Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers, because they change their environment more dramatically than almost any other animal apart from humans. By building dams across streams, they create ponds and wetlands. These slow down the flow of water after heavy rain, which can reduce the risk of flooding in towns and villages further downstream. The ponds also trap soil that has been washed off farmland, along with the chemicals it contains, so the water that flows out of beaver wetlands is often much cleaner than the water that flows in. A single family of beavers can build several dams along a short stretch of stream, and over time these can turn a narrow, fast-flowing channel into a complex network of pools and channels. Lecturer: The wetlands themselves support a huge variety of wildlife. Numbers of amphibians such as frogs increase, as do insects, and the insects in turn attract bats, which can often be seen hunting over beaver ponds at dusk. Some studies have found many more species living along streams with beavers than along similar streams without them. Dead trees standing in the water also provide nesting sites for birds such as woodpeckers. Lecturer: However, releasing beavers needs careful planning. The first requirement is a site with a good supply of food. Contrary to popular belief, beavers don't eat fish. They're vegetarian, and in winter they depend largely on the bark of trees, especially willow, which grows quickly and regrows after it has been cut. Secondly, it's essential to talk to farmers before any release takes place. Beaver dams can flood fields, and beavers sometimes feed on crops, so farmers need to know what to expect and how any problems will be dealt with. It's also important to check that the river system is large enough to support several families, because young beavers leave home at around two years old and need to find territories of their own. Lecturer: Beavers can also cause trouble by blocking drains under roads, which can lead to flooding in the wrong places. Fortunately, there are solutions. One of the most effective is to install pipes through the dam, which control the level of water in the pond without the dam having to be removed altogether. Lecturer: Now let's look at two examples. In 2013, a family of wild beavers was discovered living on the River Otter in Devon, in south-west England. Nobody knows exactly where they came from, but they're thought to have escaped from a private collection. The government agreed to a five-year trial, and the results were so positive that in 2020 the beavers were given permission to stay permanently, making them the first legally recognised wild population in England. Researchers found that the dams had reduced peak water flows during storms, helping to protect a village downstream. They also found that the beavers had brought new income to the area, thanks to an increase in tourism, as people came from all over the country hoping to catch a glimpse of them. Lecturer: In Scotland, beavers were officially reintroduced in Argyll in 2009, and in 2019 they became a legally protected species there. One of the most successful aspects of the Scottish projects has been the involvement of local communities. Volunteers help to monitor the beavers using cameras hidden near their lodges and dams, which record their activity at night, and local schools use the footage in their lessons. This kind of involvement helps people to feel that the beavers belong to them, and that makes a real difference when conflicts arise. In the second half of the lecture, we'll look at some of those conflicts in more detail. That is the end of Part 4. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
